background:
Jude: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes

Study notes · dates are approximate and scholars vary

At a glance

Jude is a short, urgent letter. Jude had planned to write about “our common salvation,” but instead had to warn believers to “contend earnestly for the faith” against ungodly teachers who had crept in. It probably dates from about AD 65–80.

QuestionTraditional viewNotes
Author“Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James” (v. 1)Traditionally Judas, one of Jesus' brothers (Mark 6:3), who like James came to faith after the resurrection (Acts 1:14).
DateAbout AD 65–80Uncertain; it is closely related to 2 Peter 2.
Recipients“Them that are called” (v. 1)Probably Jewish Christians who knew the Old Testament and Jewish traditions well.
The problemUngodly people “turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness” (v. 4)They rejected authority, followed their desires and caused divisions.
SourcesQuotes 1 Enoch (vv. 14–15) and alludes to the Assumption of Moses (v. 9)Jewish writings well known in the first century, though not part of the Hebrew Bible.
EndingOne of the Bible's best-known doxologies (vv. 24–25)“Now unto him that is able to guard you from stumbling.”

Jude is built in triplets: three examples of judgment (vv. 5–7), three types of rebels (v. 11), and three groups to be helped (vv. 22–23).

The time map

The shaded band marks the likely period of writing. The exact date is uncertain.

Jude's Jewish and Roman world

Jude writes as a Jewish Christian, steeped in Scripture and Jewish tradition, to believers facing moral and spiritual danger.

  • 1 Enoch. A collection of Jewish writings from the last centuries BC, widely read in Jesus' day; copies were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. Jude quotes its prophecy of the Lord coming with His holy ones (vv. 14–15).
  • Michael and Moses. Jude's reference to the archangel Michael disputing with the devil over Moses' body (v. 9) comes from a Jewish writing, the Assumption (or Testament) of Moses.
  • Fallen angels. Jewish tradition, based on Genesis 6, told of angels who left their proper place and were bound in darkness (v. 6).
  • Love feasts. Early Christians shared meals together, called “love-feasts” (v. 12). The false teachers joined these meals and used them for self-indulgence.
  • A culture of indulgence. Roman banquets and pagan festivals often involved drinking and sexual immorality, which these teachers excused in the name of grace.
  • A family under watch. A later tradition says Domitian questioned Jude's grandsons as descendants of David, and released them when he saw their calloused farmers' hands.

Against people who “set at nought dominion” (v. 8), Jude points to God's past judgments as a warning and to His power to keep the faithful.

The places behind Jude's warnings

Jude's examples are drawn from Israel's history and the lands around Judea.

  • Egypt and the wilderness. The Lord saved Israel out of Egypt, yet later destroyed those who did not believe (v. 5).
  • Sodom and Gomorrah. Traditionally located near the southern end of the Dead Sea, destroyed for their immorality (v. 7).
  • Cain. The first murderer (v. 11; Gen 4).
  • Balaam. The prophet from Mesopotamia hired by the king of Moab to curse Israel, who led them into sin for profit (v. 11; Num 22–25).
  • Korah. Rebelled against Moses in the wilderness and was swallowed by the earth (v. 11; Num 16).
  • Galilee and Jerusalem. Jude grew up in Nazareth with Jesus and James; his brother James led the Jerusalem church.

Maps: then and now

Jude's examples come from the lands around Judea: Egypt, the Sinai wilderness, the Dead Sea region and Moab.

Today these lands belong to Egypt, Israel, the West Bank and Jordan.

Around the world in the AD 60s–70s

Jude was written during a time of upheaval.

RegionWhat was happening
RomeNero's persecution (AD 64), the Year of the Four Emperors (AD 69) and the rise of Vespasian.
JudeaThe Jewish revolt (AD 66–70) ended with Jerusalem and the temple destroyed; Masada fell in AD 73 or 74.
BritainRoman conquest pushed into Wales and the north.
ItalyVesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum in AD 79.
ChinaThe Eastern Han dynasty; Ban Chao began campaigns to reopen the Silk Road in AD 73.
The AmericasTeotihuacan was growing in central Mexico.

How the setting shapes the study

Jude draws on writings and customs its readers knew well.

PassageConnection to the times
Jude 4“Crept in privily”: traveling teachers could join house churches easily.
Jude 6Jewish tradition from Genesis 6 told of angels kept in darkness for judgment.
Jude 9The dispute over Moses' body comes from the Assumption of Moses.
Jude 12“Love-feasts” were shared church meals; the false teachers turned them into banquets.
Jude 12–13Images from nature: waterless clouds, fruitless trees, wild waves and wandering stars.
Jude 14–15Jude quotes 1 Enoch 1:9, a book found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.
Jude 24–25Doxologies like this were spoken in synagogue and church worship.

After all its warnings, Jude ends with God's power “to guard you from stumbling, and to set you before the presence of his glory without blemish in exceeding joy” (v. 24).

items.text: Greeting vv. 1–2
Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James, to them that are called, beloved in God the Father, and kept for Jesus Christ:
Mercy unto you and peace and love be multiplied.
Contend for the Faith vv. 3–4

Beloved, while I was giving all diligence to write unto you of our common salvation, I was constrained to write unto you exhorting you to contend earnestly for the faith which was once for all delivered unto the saints.

For there are certain men crept in privily, even they who were of old written of beforehand unto this condemnation, ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness, and denying our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.
Judgment on the Ungodly vv. 5–16
Now I desire to put you in remembrance, though ye know all things once for all, that the Lord, having saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed them that believed not.
And angels that kept not their own principality, but left their proper habitation, he hath kept in everlasting bonds under darkness unto the judgment of the great day.

Even as Sodom and Gomorrah, and the cities about them, having in like manner with these given themselves over to fornication and gone after strange flesh, are set forth as an example, suffering the punishment of eternal fire.
Yet in like manner these also in their dreamings defile the flesh, and set at nought dominion, and rail at dignities.
But Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing judgment, but said, The Lord rebuke thee.
But these rail at whatsoever things they know not: and what they understand naturally, like the creatures without reason, in these things are they destroyed.
Woe unto them! for they went in the way of Cain, and ran riotously in the error of Balaam for hire, and perished in the gainsaying of Korah.

These are they who are hidden rocks in your love-feasts when they feast with you, shepherds that without fear feed themselves; clouds without water, carried along by winds; autumn trees without fruit, twice dead, plucked up by the roots;
wild waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, for whom the blackness of darkness hath been reserved for ever.
And to these also Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying, Behold, the Lord came with ten thousands of his holy ones,

to execute judgment upon all, and to convict all the ungodly of all their works of ungodliness which they have ungodly wrought, and of all the hard things which ungodly sinners have spoken against him.
These are murmurers, complainers, walking after their lusts (and their mouth speaketh great swelling words), showing respect of persons for the sake of advantage.
A Call to Persevere vv. 17–23
But ye, beloved, remember ye the words which have been spoken before by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ;
that they said to you, In the last time there shall be mockers, walking after their own ungodly lusts.
These are they who make separations, sensual, having not the Spirit.
But ye, beloved, building up yourselves on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit,
keep yourselves in the love of God, looking for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life.
And on some have mercy, who are in doubt;
and some save, snatching them out of the fire; and on some have mercy with fear; hating even the garment spotted by the flesh.
Doxology vv. 24–25
Now unto him that is able to guard you from stumbling, and to set you before the presence of his glory without blemish in exceeding joy,
to the only God our Saviour, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion and power, before all time, and now, and for evermore. Amen.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: What examples from Israel's history and Jewish tradition does Jude use in vv. 5–11 to describe the ungodly people who had crept in?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: Why would readers familiar with writings like 1 Enoch find the prophecy quoted in vv. 14–15 a fitting warning about the intruders at their love-feasts?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Jude urges building yourselves up, praying, keeping in God's love and showing mercy (vv. 20–23); which of these does your faith most need now?

wrap.title: Jude In Summary
paras: Jude is a short, urgent letter from the brother of James and of Jesus. He had wanted to write about the salvation all believers share, but felt compelled instead to urge them to “contend earnestly for the faith which was once for all delivered unto the saints.” Certain ungodly people had slipped in among them, turning God's grace into an excuse for immorality and denying the Lord Jesus Christ.

To show that God judges such people, Jude reminds his readers of examples from the past: Israelites saved from Egypt but later destroyed for unbelief, angels who left their proper place and are kept in darkness for judgment, and Sodom and Gomorrah, punished for their immorality. The false teachers follow the way of Cain, the greed of Balaam and the rebellion of Korah.

Jude describes these teachers with vivid images: hidden rocks at the church's love feasts, clouds without water, trees without fruit, wild waves foaming out their shame, wandering stars. Quoting the ancient prophecy of Enoch, he warns that the Lord will come with His holy ones to judge the ungodly. They grumble, follow their own desires, flatter for gain and cause divisions.

But Jude turns to his “beloved” with encouragement. They should remember the apostles' warnings, build themselves up in their most holy faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in God's love and wait for the mercy of the Lord Jesus Christ. They must show mercy to those who doubt, rescue others as if from fire, and show mercy with caution. The letter ends with a magnificent doxology to God, who is able to keep them from stumbling and to present them faultless before His glory with great joy. The message in one line: believers must stand firm for the true faith against those who twist grace into license, trusting the God who is able to keep them to the end.
